name: geis

attributes.attribute: is a ritual taboo that binds a named king or hero
was enforced by gods or cosmic powers, not by courts
is linked etymologically to the verb guidid, 'prays, asks'
has a Welsh counterpart in the swearing of destiny
broke his gessa and met death at Da Derga's hostel

sources: Dillon, Myles. There Was a King in Ireland: Five Tales from Oral Tradition. Texas Folklore Society. Austin: University of Texas Press, 1971, 21.
Joyce, Patrick Weston. Ancient Celtic Romances. London: Parkgate Books, 1997, 433–434.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: A geis is a ritual prohibition in early Irish literature, and the plural is gessa. The word names a taboo or sworn injunction that binds a named person, most often a king or a hero. Scholars link it to the verb guidid, 'prays' or 'asks', so the taboo began as a formal request. Welsh gwŷs, 'summons', may come from the same Common Celtic formation. Irish texts also use other words for the same idea, among them airmit and airgart. No court or lawman enforced geasa. The narrative holds that gods, the heroic code, or unnamed cosmic powers made them bite. Most gessa came at birth or when a person took up a new role, so breaking one undid that person's own nature. The tales use the pattern to mark a hero's doom in advance. King Conaire Mór of Tara carried a string of prohibitions: no hunting of the birds of the air, no night away from Tara, no entry by three red riders. He broke them one by one, and the breaking led to his death in Togail Bruidne Da Derga. Some scholars think the idea came from the Bible, while others argue for a native Irish institution. A Welsh parallel appears in the swearing of destiny in the Welsh tales Math and Culhwch ac Olwen. The concept joined magical force to social duty, and it shaped how storytellers built a hero's rise and fall.

okr.objective: Explain the Irish ritual prohibition called geis, its origin, its enforcement, and its narrative work.
key_results: Define geis and its plural gessa as a binding taboo.
Give the proposed etymology from guidid and the Welsh cognate gwŷs.
Show how Conaire Mór's broken gessa drive the plot of Togail Bruidne Da Derga.
Compare the Irish concept with the Welsh swearing of destiny.
